A trembling hand fumbles in the scratchy wool of an overcoat pocket for another five-round clip. That damned bolt again. The last round stuck fast. One strike. Another—with a numb palm. New clip…stiff bolt handle forward and down…chamber a new round and close the breech.
So cold. Eyes ache from peering into the fogged dark. The head throbs from gunfire crackling since morning.
A minor railway stop, Kruty, lost in bleak fields, near a nameless hamlet beyond Nizhyn.

“They’re coming, still coming, stay alert!” officers shout hoarsely from the snow-covered embankment, voices strained. Through icy fog and under the dim light of a veiled moon, shadows advance across the wide field, cut through by endless rails.
The Reds send another wave into the attack.
A flash splits the darkness on the far horizon. Then a boom, and an explosion close by. The blasts throb like a pulse in the temples.
Teeth clench. The head pulls inward, wishing never to hear and see, shrapnel whistles overhead. This time for sure.
A hoarse shout—the machine guns burst to life, tearing the darkness with short volleys, chewing through belts of cartridges.
Around, thin lines of defense stretch across the silvery ribbon of rails: a motley battalion of whoever God sent, in whatever they had, with God knows-what instead of proper weapons.

Students from Kyiv. Young cadets in old overcoats, in felt boots, with grimy yellow-blue armbands on their sleeves. Gymnasium students, mere schoolboys who had hardly ever fired a shot before, in ordinary clothes, standing off to the left to keep away from harm. Fiery, dreamy lads who did not run, too ashamed to turn their backs.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.

One student—his face still untouched by a razor—keeps nervously adjusting his round spectacles again and again, brushing frost-dust with trembling fingers. They had all volunteered. Shivering in the cold, breathing heavily. Clumsily digging shallow trenches. They weren’t meant to be here. Schoolboys, maybe good enough to haul ammo, nothing more. So they were sent to a “relatively quiet sector” of the front, but ended up encountering the main enemy forces.

A handful of junior officers, none over thirty, stand beside them in Russian army uniforms, their epaulets torn off, imperial cockades missing. This was the young army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic—its most devoted part.
“Matviy, keep an eye on the youngsters here!” A gloved hand claps his shoulder, and the officer ducks low, moving on to steady the thin line.

Another deep, dull thud, one that rings sharp in the skull, not just the ears. The soft stubble of a cheek touches the frozen wooden stock again. Lungs pull in frost. Another shot into the darkness merges into the deafening cannonade. And another. And again.

They keep coming with bayonets fixed, advancing toward the machine guns across the field to the station. Navy peacoats, quilted jackets, caps, red armbands. They’ve been coming since morning. Sailors of the Baltic Fleet. Red Guards from Petrograd and Moscow…no strangers to this kind of work.

The Reds are advancing on Kyiv.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.
Kharkiv is lost, Poltava is lost, Chernihiv is lost. Through forests and steppe, along rails from Russia, the armored trains grind toward the Ukrainian capital.
Another heavy blow from the Bolshevik battery—and now they’re pulling him away: sotnyk Omelchenko, the student company leader, his head torn open by shrapnel, blood gushing from beneath his cap.
You won’t make it to Kyiv, friend. Remember us up there.
We can’t hold this alone. Not for long.

Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.
What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life , “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:
Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.
When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.
The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself . Pärt puts it more gently:
One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book.
If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.
I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:
Silence with you is like the faint delicious
Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed:
Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming,
The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest.
Silence with you is like a kind departure
From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd
Into a wide and greenly barren meadow,
Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud;
Or like one held upon the sands at evening,
When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light
Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed
Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

A self is a forest . A self is a ship . A self is an illusion , and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves , contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life , takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman ( public library | free ebook ).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. Union Veterans and the Bitter Aftermath of the Civil War
As the nation embraced reconciliation, former Union soldiers questioned whether their sacrifices had been in vain.

In the decade following the Civil War, many white northerners wanted nothing more than to put the carnage behind them and reunify the country. But, historian Brian Matthew Jordan writes, one group that generally wasn’t ready to forgive and forget was Union veterans.

Jordan writes that the returning soldiers found a society that was happy to hail them as heroes but often offered them little material support. Many employers refused to hire men who they believed were too mentally or physically wounded to function.

And veterans’ efforts to ask for more were frequently dismissed. In the summer of 1865, just months after the war’s end, The New York Times complained that returning military men “prefer to live by begging.”

But Jordan argues that the veterans’ anger was not just about their own needs. Many felt that efforts to move past the conflict insulted their sacrifices. Those who returned with disabilities, painful wounds, and post-traumatic stress were reminded constantly of the war, and some worked to remind their neighbors, staging mock battles on town greens to show the “stay at homes” what the fighting had looked like. One wrote that “the momentous events of less than ten years ago are too fresh in memory to be forgotten at the command of any party that may be benefitted by ignoring them.”
The images, diaries, and ephemera in Grand Valley State University’s Civil War and Slavery Collection reveal the cold realities of Abraham Lincoln’s world.

A prime symbol of this neglect for many was the Confederacy’s president, Jefferson Davis . Soon after the war’s end, one veteran wrote to President Andrew Johnson, saying that he believed he had been “spared to witness the close of this wicked and unjust rebellion” and would be honored to help build a scaffold for Davis’s execution. Instead, despite being accused of treason, Davis was released two years after the war’s end and became a symbol of the Lost Cause . One Union veteran from Massachusetts complained that he had lost an arm “in vain” since “Jefferson Davis is today a hero, and more care is taken of him than the soldiers who fought to preserve the Union.”

Jordan writes that the Grand Army of the Republic (GAR), which was founded in 1866 and quickly became a national organization with 2,000 posts, focused primarily on supporting veterans, widows, and orphans, including by lobbying for benefits. But it also protested the appointment of “rebels and traitors” to government offices that could have gone to former Union soldiers.
GAR soon became a controversial group, with some northern civilians arguing that its demands and remembrances kept too much bitterness alive and made it difficult for the country to move forward.

In some cases, military service had also introduced northern soldiers to ideas about racial justice that their neighbors back home didn’t embrace . While not every white veteran became a supporter of Black Americans’ rights, Jordan suggests that it wasn’t uncommon. As the planter class attempted to reinstate a system of virtual slavery with the Black Codes and vigilante violence, some wondered if they would end up having to fight the war all over again.

At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane .”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story , which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman . Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature , the directorial debut of Jules Dassin , an animated short narrated by James Mason , a British psychological thriller , and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes .

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “ Floating University ” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne , the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists , “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences . It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma.

When Colorado Closed Its Border to New Mexico
An anti-immigrant stunt in 1936 helped propel a governor to the US Senate, despite its limited practical impact.

By the 1930s, the federal government was in charge of immigration, having centralized and formalized the ad hoc immigration regimes cities and states had developed during the nineteenth century. So it was news in April 1936, when Colorado Governor Edwin C. “Big Ed” Johnson declared martial law along the border with… the neighboring state of New Mexico. Johnson publicized his action as a blockade to stop a supposed “invasion” of “alien and indigent persons.”

When his earlier proposal to set up concentration camps for Mexican immigrant workers, who were pressing for higher wages in the sugar beet industry, came to naught, he hit upon the border blockade gambit. Political scientist Monica W. Varsanyi writes of Johnson’s “ classic example of political entrepreneurship ”:

Although his plans had little actual impact on Colorado’s agricultural labor market or welfare relief load, they resulted in an outpouring of public support, which he exploited in his successful run for the US Senate later in 1936.”

Beyond yet another precedent for the political benefits of racism and nativism, Johnson’s actions present a case study of racialization, the political and ideological process of race-making and the creation of color lines. The militarized race border between two US states, continues Varsanyi:

created circumstances in which the social boundary between who belonged and who fell outside of citizenship and belonging was both heightened and vigorously contested in this uniquely multi-ethnic region populated by Anglos, native-born Hispanics, Mexican immigrants, and Native Americans.

American citizenship had originally been granted to “free white” persons in the Naturalization Act of 1790. The territory conquered in the Mexican – American War added at least 80,000 people to the rolls of American citizenship in 1848 . These Mexican Americans and their descendants therefore were considered white in federal law. But this was a precarious whiteness. In the Southwest, Mexican Americans were second-class citizens. Regardless of de jure law, Anglos did not see them as white and treated them accordingly . “Juan Crow” segregation covered housing, education, and employment.

Varsanyi quotes Colorado resident and US citizen Filigonio Arellano, “During wartime and when they need my vote, white people call me an American. If I need a loan, I am Spanish. And if I’m applying for a job they call me Mexican.”

Nonetheless, Johnson’s blockade received a good bit of support from native-born Hispanics. These US citizens tried to distinguish themselves as “Spanish Americans” or “Hispanos” in opposition to Mexicans. “Spanish-speaking New Mexicans, elite and impoverished alike, rebuffed claims of mestizo , ‘impure,’ or ‘mixed’ blood by tracing their lineage back to Europe and Spain, not Mexico.”
Birth of A National Immigration Policy
Until the Civil War, regulating immigration to the US was left to individual states. That changed with Emancipation and the legal end of slavery.

There was some “solidarity between Hispanic and Mexican workers, mainly within the labor movement and religious communities,” but otherwise little sense of a “pan ethnic/pan-Hispanic solidarity or ‘Mexicanness.’”

Of course, to a racist, birthplace or citizenship hardly mattered. New Mexico residents who were US citizens who tried going north for work in Colorado’s sugar beet, railroad, mining, and sheep-herding industries, as they had for decades, found that they were classified as “aliens” and “Mexicans” and turned back.

The blockade only lasted eleven days. Pressure from the powerful sugar beet interests—who could not get white Coloradans to work under the industry’s brutal conditions—and rising tensions with New Mexico likely led Johnson to call it off. A marked increase in racism persisted long after, however.

Johnson himself would go on to serve three terms in the US Senate before becoming Colorado governor again in 1955. How Magic Lantern Ghosts Helped Measure the Stars
A nineteenth-century invention brought theatrical illusions into the observatory, changing how astronomers studied starlight.

In the nineteenth century, entertainers began dazzling audiences with the “magic lantern.” Operators used these projection systems to bring marvelous images to large crowds. They even performed tricks on the eye, conjuring “ghosts” onto the stage using reflections or transparent screens. But some at the time saw scientific possibilities in those ghostly images.

The rise of projection culture coincided with an increasing effort to mechanize astronomy . Astronomers had been precisely charting the positions of stars and other objects, and the next step was to study their color and brightness. German projectionist Karl Friedrich Zöllner realized that magic lanterns might help astronomers in this effort, explains historian Klaus Staubermann . He argues that Zöllner’s new scientific instrument, an astro-photometer, harnessed the subjective perception created by the magic lantern for scientific purposes.

The principles behind the “magic lantern” have a deep history, but improvements by Christiaan Huygens and others in the seventeenth century led to more widespread use. Staubermann describes how magic lanterns became popular lecture aids by the eighteenth century, as improvements to lighting and mirrors made them suitable for larger theaters. Projectionists learned new ways to control brightness and create visual effects using a variety of filters and lenses. Meanwhile, scientists were experimenting with optics, prisms, and mineralogy.

It was in this milieu that Zöllner became a projectionist and a student of photometry. He began studying illusions, trying to understand how we distinguish them from reality. He thought of the retina itself as a projection screen, Staubermann explains. To Zöllner, “The mind was the spectator,” he writes, “looking at the image and deciding what of that which was seen was illusory and what was real.”
The Hidden Aesthetics of Early Astrophotography
Behind the transformative star photographs of the 1880s lay a complex collaboration between astronomers and engravers.

It was the interplay between reality and illusion that enabled Zöllner’s photometer. The instrument employed techniques similar to those used to conjure ghosts on the stage to create artificial stars. A gas burner provided intense and steady light, which was projected as a point of light on a semi-transparent glass screen using lenses and prisms.

“For the observer with a Zöllner photometer,” Staubermann writes, “it appeared as if both stars were actually in the sky, having the same background.” The operator could control the brightness of the “ghost” star and compare it with a real one. Previously, astronomers’ perceptions of star brightness and color varied, sometimes significantly. But as they began experimenting with Zöllner’s photometer, they obtained results that agreed with each other.

The instrument became a best seller in Europe and the United States. Astronomers added it to telescopes like the one at Leipzig Observatory. By the 1870s, Staubermann explains, “of the observatories participating in international observing programmes almost half of them had ordered a Zöllner photometer.” Papers on astro-photometry proliferated, and Zöllner himself became the first German professor of astrophysics.

Staubermann argues that the photometer didn’t quite make astro-photometry a “mechanically objective” science, however. Using it meant refining observation skills rather than eliminating the need for them. “Through the use of Zöllner’s photometer,” he writes, “observers learned how to both control and improve their visual judgement.”

While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and…
A food studies scholar provides some tips for throwing the perfect Friendsgiving gathering.

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Mogging is the word of the year – but men have been doing it since Shakespearean times
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.
The Collins English Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year.

The Collins website says that the word originated with the acronym AMOG – or “alpha male of the group” – which is often associated with bodybuilding forums and, more recently, the toxic culture of incels and the manosphere . But mogging has now entered mainstream language with its meaning slightly repurposed: to describe someone who is outperforming, outshining or upstaging someone.

While the verb is often used in reference to physical looks, it can also be applied in other contexts. Alex Beecroft , managing director of Collins, explained that the selection of mogging demonstrates how “each generation leaves its mark on language”, with the term seeing a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.

The Oxford English Dictionary contains four historic meanings of the base verb “mog”. The earliest meaning and usage comes as early as 1674, referring to card games “to exchange a card with the dealer”. A later usage means “to move on, depart, decamp”. By the mid-1800s, two new possible meanings emerged : “to walk slowly but steadily” and “to shift (a person, animal etc.) to cause to move on (esp. quickly)”.

What unites these historic meanings is the connection to movement or performance. For many men in the early modern period, the demonstration of superiority through action and movement was a key method to showcase, or perhaps fittingly, “mog” others.

New research by theatre historian Eleanor Rycroft explores this link between movement, gender and social power. Rycroft examines theatrical works by playwrights such as Shakespeare and Ben Jonson alongside historical conduct books and household management guides, revealing just how much cultural capital was attached to a man’s posture and stride.

How-to guides and etiquette books from the time told men and women how to behave, labelling certain traits as respectable and others as improper. In the 1566 English translation of Ortensio Landi’s Delectable Demaundes and Pleasaunt Questions (1566), readers were shown how to outdo other men in wit and conduct. Yet in doing so, the text also exposed the cracks in this ideal, revealing how precarious that masculine status truly was.

In his influential Book of the Courtier (1528), courtier and diplomat Baldassare Castiglione defined this quality as a “certain nonchalance, which shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought”.
Sprezzatura in Shakespeare and asserting manhood
Castiglione was first translated into English by Sir Thomas Hoby in 1561, and the concept of sprezzatura heavily influenced early modern English culture.

In many early modern plays, characters demonstrate the importance of asserting a mastery of manhood and, with it, upstaging others. While Shakespeare does not use the terms sprezzatura or mogging in any of his works, many men attempt to outperform or outshine other characters to assert or affirm their manly status.

In Much Ado About Nothing (first performed 1598), the “merry war” between protagonists Beatrice and Benedick – a rapid-fire exchange loaded with insults as the two characters shield their true feelings for one another – is often a source of audience amusement and laughter. However, this “skirmish of wit” points to the different expectations on men and women for Benedick across the play text: to match and ideally best Beatrice’s skill in wordplay so as not to emasculate himself.

Beatrice seems to be aware of these dynamics of masculinity, noting that Benedick “gets nothing” from their verbal exchanges – after their last encounter, “four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one”. These scenes of verbal sparring might be understood as a trial of masculinity, testing Benedick’s skills in rhetoric and wordplay.

East Germany exiled singer Wolf Biermann. They only made his message louder
Fifty years ago the GDR withdrew the citizenship of the prominent leftwing dissident. It turned him into an international symbol – and cemented his place in history

November 16 marks 50 years since one of the most notorious examples of artistic censorship from the 20th century: the East German government’s stripping the citizenship of dissident singer-songwriter Wolf Biermann .
Far from quashing Biermann’s voice, this act of political exile amplified it, and cemented his place in history, underscored by a new documentary about his life story.

It is a lesson others should have done more to heed. Earlier this year, US billionaire Robert Kraft and other stadium owners banned Macklemore from their venues over pro-Palestinian remarks the singer made during his support slot on Ed Sheeran’s tour.
But in trying to silence the rapper, Kraft and his cohort unintentionally amplified his message .
The story of Biermann can tell us much about how attempts to quash the political expression of musicians have spectacularly backfired.
From East German darling to dissident
Biermann, born in 1936, became a prominent figure within East German left-wing dissident artists and intellectuals in the late 1960s. But he wasn’t always an outsider.

As the West German immigrant son of a Jewish communist killed in Auschwitz, and a mentee of Bertolt Brecht, Biermann was initially the darling of the East German press, and held a candidate membership of the Socialist Unity Party (SED).

When his lyrics became critical of the SED, however, the Stasi (secret police) began a campaign of harassment that escalated over more than a decade. It included performance bans, sabotage, intimidation, round-the-clock surveillance, bugging, reports from more than 200 Stasi informants , and even a veiled death threat.
Yet this persecution amplified Biermann’s voice and gave him an international platform.
The making of an international symbol
Western governments adopted Biermann as a potent symbol in the cultural Cold War. He acquired famous fans, including Joan Baez and Allen Ginsberg.
Numerous organisations awarded him prizes. CBS gave him a record deal, and West Berlin radio stations frequently broadcast his music into East Germany.

These broadcasts made some remarkable converts. Gerulf Pannach, a young songwriter and then Stasi informant , first heard Biermann’s music while working as a border guard. He befriended the singer, renounced the Stasi and began writing his own critical lyrics.
Pannach convinced Christian Kunert, the keyboardist of the beloved rock band Renft , to take an anti-state position in 1974.

Kunert, in turn, introduced writer and social psychologist Jürgen Fuchs – who would go on to become a prominent East German dissident – to Pannach and Biermann. He also converted his Renft band mate Thomas “Monster” Schoppe to the cause.
Closer to home, Biermann’s former stepdaughter, young rock singer and future queen of punk Nina Hagen , introduced her bandmates to Biermann.

Biermann’s inner circle was, for a time, paradoxically protected by their fame as dissidents. Aided by Western media, they flouted state controls in ways average East Germans wouldn’t dare. While the state maintained tight surveillance of Biermann’s circle, they seemed hesitant to arrest them.
But those more loosely associated with Biermann often found themselves caught in the crossfire of multiple Stasi operations to harass and crush dissidents.
This included band members of Renft, who helped Pannach bypass his performance ban and perform Biermann’s songs, and publicly denounced East German border policy.
As a result, members of Renft were repeatedly summoned and questioned by the authorities. Then the band was banned. In September 1975, a local licensing board told Renft they “no longer exist”.
Taboo themes in Pannach’s lyrics were the pretext for the ban , but declassified Stasi documents suggest the state ultimately targeted them as proxies for Biermann.
The regime accidentally elevated a popular East German rock band to anti-state legends.

A further attempt to neutralise Renft through conscription and a tax investigation converted the band’s thus far apolitical founder, Klaus Jentzsch, into a gifted anti-state organiser. With Biermann’s help, he coordinated a transnational multi-media campaign.

Meet the bears of Anan Creek
Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises ), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan , 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears ( Ursus americanus ) and eight brown bears ( Ursus arctos) . Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai , every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

In addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home . Bald eagles ( Haliaeetus leucocephalus ), the Alexander Archipelago wolf ( Canis lupus ligoni ), and the Sitka black-tailed deer ( Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis ). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon ( Oncorhynchus tshawytscha ), coho ( Oncorhynchus kisutch ), pink ( Oncorhynchus gorbuscha ), sockeye ( Oncorhynchus nerka ), and chum ( Oncorhynchus keta ). Clam discovered living inside of a sea urchin’s throat
The deep-sea duo has an unusual arrangement.

The fact that a new clam species ( Vaticinaria gulicola ) was discovered where the sun does not shine may be the least interesting thing about this bivalve. V. gulicola lives inside of a deep-sea urchin . The clam appears to have made a little home for itself inside the urchin’s oesophagus, the tube that runs through the center of the urchin’s body and into the intestine. A study recently published in the journal ZooKeys details this highly unusual partnership.

An international team of scientists conducting a deep-sea survey of the Great Australian Bight discovered the clam. The survey studied the seafloor at depths of 656 to 16,404 feet deep and uncovered 66,721 invertebrates representing 1,267 species. About a third of these species are believed to be new to science—including this quirky clam.

They found V. gulicola along the abyssal seafloor at depths of about 13,000 to 16,400 feet. At this depth, sunlight cannot penetrate the water column . During these deep trawls, the team found clams equipped with threads for attaching to a host, but did not see any hosts. Additional searching revealed more clams lodged inside thin, slippery tubes. They analyzed the DNA of these tubes and discovered that they were the oesophagus of the urchin Carnarechinus clypeatus.

“We were absolutely stunned to find this bivalve living inside the throat of a deepwater sea urchin,” Paul Valentich-Scott , a study co-author and marine malacologist at the Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History, said in a statement . “A Russian scientist [Alexander Mironov] originally thought these clams were being eaten by the sea urchin, but we later determined that it was actually living inside the oesophagus.”

Mironov had noticed clams inside the urchin’s gut as far back as the 1970s and 1990s. The team also found related clams living inside of a specimen of the same urchin that was collected during the Challenger Expedition (1872 to 1876), where they had gone unnoticed for over a century.

Most clam species that live with other animals cling to the outside of their host. Endocommensalism , or living inside of the host, is more rare. The new clam’s genus Vaticinaria is only the second clam genus of its superfamily known to live this way.
“Endocommensalism is extremely rare in galeommatids and all bivalves,” Valentich-Scott added. “Most commensal bivalves attach to the outside of their host. This new species lives inside its throat.”

This new clam shows no obvious adaptations to life inside a host. It is about 0.74 inches long, which is large for its group, and has a shell that closes fully. The species name gulicola comes from the Latin word for “throat” and “inhabitant.” Much about the clam remains unknown and will require further study.

“We know very little about this new species or its sea urchin host,” said Valentich-Scott. “The host sea urchin has never been collected intact, so we really don’t even know what it looks like. We have no idea how this bivalve can live inside the throat of the urchin, or what it eats.”

The team suspects that the clams can feed off the nutrient-rich sediment that the urchin eats, but this hasn’t been studied. Further deep-sea sampling should reveal more about this clam and other unusual creatures of the deep-sea.

How Humans Are Helping Golden Jackals Conquer Europe
By unintentionally protecting jackals from larger predators, people are aiding in the expansion of a remarkably adaptable canid.

The golden jackal isn’t always the color of gold; its coat ranges from creamy beige to a rusty brown with black striations. It is, however, living in a golden age—thanks in part to the ubiquity of humans.

Native to Eurasia, golden jackals in Europe have historically been confined to the southeastern tips of the continent, mainly the Balkan countries. Over the past century, though, Canis aureus has slowly started colonizing new areas of Europe, with a steep acceleration over the past two decades. Golden jackals are expanding their range, reaching as far west as Spain and as far north as the Arctic. Scientists say the expansion represents one of the most dramatic changes in the range of a species in today’s world. New research, including genetic analysis, is revealing what’s driving the jackal’s spread and the part people play in the animal’s success.

One factor that has contributed to golden jackals’ expansion is anthropogenic climate change, which has decreased snow cover and probably revealed more suitable canid habitat. The habitat fragmentation that comes with farming and urbanization is another likely influence, since golden jackals prefer a patchy environment. The species also adapts readily to human-altered landscapes and can disperse hundreds of kilometers in search of new habitat. And, not least of all, researchers suspect that humans cleared the way for them by extirpating wolves across much of Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.
“The fact that they did not have any competitor made it easier,” says Jennifer Hatlauf, a wildlife ecologist who manages the Golden Jackal Project in Austria .

Today, researchers estimate that around 150,000 golden jackals inhabit 23 European countries, populating a range that’s 46 percent bigger than it was in 2016 . But wolf populations are growing, too; Europe hosts roughly 23,000 wolves today, compared to an estimated 12,000 as recently as 2012.

To better understand how humans, a growing wolf population, and the expanding golden jackal population interact, Hatlauf and a large team of researchers collected and analyzed data on the presence of golden jackals from all around Europe between 2001 and 2017. The information mainly came from playback surveys: Researchers played a jackal call from a speaker and listened for the response of real jackals, identifying the presence of individuals. The team then paired this data with data on wolf and human presence.

Their recently published analysis shows that the presence of wolves is the main factor limiting the expansion of jackals—a result that strengthens the hypothesis that the decline of wolves in past centuries likely opened the door to the jackal expansion. The team also found that human settlements create a shield that deters wolves and offers a refuge for jackals.

The “human shield” hypothesis isn’t new. Researchers have long known that prey or smaller predators take advantage of human presence to escape large predators. For example, some bear mothers with cubs find refuge from adult male bears by moving close to human settlements, especially during the mating season, when the males would try to kill offspring. Prey animals, such as wild turkeys, also seem to find safety near human-inhabited areas.

In places where wolves are absent, the data shows, jackals tend to stay away from humans, likely to avoid deadly encounters with our species. But where wolves are rooted in the landscape, jackals remain within humans’ proximity. “The jackal is three times smaller, so there’s simply no chance for a jackal if you have a core area of wolf populations,” says Hatlauf. That same life strategy is probably going to apply in other areas that jackals will reach in the future as they expand even farther, she adds.

“The work is excellent,” says Luigi Boitani, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Large Carnivore Initiative for Europe, who wasn’t involved in the research. The idea that the wolf’s extirpation played a role in the jackal’s expansion and that human presence shapes the relationship between the two species has long crossed scientists’ minds, Boitani says, but no one was able to prove it with actual data until now.

Hummingbirds often use their bills for fighting, but some species’ outsized appendages are equally useful in finding food.

Despite their diminutive size and zany colors, many hummingbird species are downright ferocious when they encounter one another at a food source. That’s likely because of the demands of their lightning-fast metabolisms. In flight, a hummingbird may flap its wings 62 times per second, and some species have heart rates that top out at over 1,200 beats per minute. Hummingbirds’ small bodies have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and they lack insulating down, so they also lose heat quickly. They must consume two to three times’ their body weight per day in high-sugar flower nectar.

Given that flowers bloom only for a short while, that makes each meal more like a high-stakes operation than a companionable feast. Even at feeders with abundant nectar supplied by humans, hummers of both sexes often joust—chasing and stabbing at each other with long, sharp bills, among other aggressive tactics and displays. The shining sunbeam ( Aglaeactis cupripennis )—on the left in this image by conservation biologist and photographer Maxime Aliaga—is no exception. Researchers tracking the species in the Andes Mountains of Peru and Ecuador found that it regularly defended flowers within its territory from hummingbirds of both its own and other species, including sword-billed hummingbirds ( Ensifera ensifera ) like the one pictured on the right.

Sword-billed hummingbirds, for their part, aren’t slouches. They wield their beaks—which are longer than their bodies—exactly as their name suggests. But the primary purpose of the species’ outsized appendage may be to get food, rather than defend it.

Scientists believe that the sword-billed hummingbird’s unique morphology evolved in tandem with long-tubed passionflowers. That subgroup within the Passiflora genus, called Tacsonia , contains more than 60 species with flower nectar tubes 6 to 14 centimeters (2 to 5 inches) long. That’s a close match with the sword-billed hummingbird’s beak, which can reach up to 11 centimeters (4 inches). The birds and flowers also overlap in range, with 37 Tacsonia species pollinated exclusively by sword-billed hummingbirds. They are the only hummingbird species with the correct proportions to deposit pollen grains on the stigmas of these dangling, downward-opening flowers, poking into them from below to drink nectar.

In intact cloud forests, this highly specialized mutualism is a boon to both plants and pollinators. But in fragmented forests, it becomes a vulnerability: Research suggests that sword-billed hummingbirds don’t frequent deforested areas. Scientists speculate that may be partly because the long-tubed passionflowers that they observed in these zones often lose their nectar to “robber” species like bees, which drill into the flowers from the side, skipping pollination and draining the hummingbirds’ food source. With the connection to the passionflowers’ primary pollinator severed, at least four species of the plant have likely gone locally extinct in landscapes fragmented by forest-clearing. Those passionflower species that have evolved shorter nectar tubes, though, are more resilient. They can rely on other hummingbirds and bats for pollination, even when the habitat becomes less suitable for sword-billed hummingbirds.

Searching for a Bird Lost to Science
A researcher grapples with the value of his efforts to document a secretive species in Papua New Guinea.

Our luck turns during a smoke break. It is hot and dry for Papua New Guinea, and we are resting on the shoulder of a gravel road, bags and cardboard biscuit boxes scattered on limestone bedrock. The boxes, in rough shape from travel, are printed with a cartoon of a man named Henry Wopa, whose bulging muscles advertise that his eponymous product is enriched with vitamins and protein. This has made the brand a staple in parts of Melanesia where deforestation has hurt food security, including here on New Britain, an island four times the size of Puerto Rico that accounts for a majority of PNG’s raw log exports . Still, the biscuits are bland and difficult to swallow without coffee, which is running out. I am hungry, but not hungry enough for more Wopa. Instead, as my colleagues squat in broken shade rolling cigarettes, I scan the canopy, ragged from decades of selective logging.

There are 10 of us in total: six Sengseng-speaking Arawe and four outsiders, including me—an evolutionary biologist from Montana—gathered to search for a poorly known bird called the New Britain bronzewing ( Henicophaps foersteri ). This large, glimmering pigeon, endemic to its namesake island, was last confirmed alive through a specimen collected by ornithologist-turned-author Jared Diamond in 1972. The bronzewing has been seen occasionally in the years since but was never again collected and has never been photographed. This is cause for some concern. As Joe Wood, an expedition member who manages international conservation programs for the Toledo Zoo & Aquarium in Ohio, put it: “It would be nice to check in on it.”

But how, exactly, do you check in on a handful of shy birds in tens of thousands of square kilometers of forest? By asking around, to start. Jason Gregg, a graduate student in my lab at Montana State University and the expedition’s leader, has spent years thinking about how to incorporate local ecological knowledge into biodiversity surveys, along with spending many hours interviewing our Arawe crew members. About half say they’re familiar with the species—known locally as kau—but communicating across gulfs of language and culture about a bird of which there are no photographs is challenging. The night before, Thomas Sunamli, who is letting us stay on his land, explained that the bronzewing is common in disturbed habitat and feeds on the red, pine-cone-like flowers of a plant called shampoo ginger ( Zingiber zerumbet ). This contradicted our own limited understanding of the bird’s diet and need for old growth.

“It’s hard to imagine what they could be getting out of [those flowers],” Wood had said, frowning as he prodded a clump of shampoo ginger at the edge of camp. Since nectar is rarely an important part of a pigeon’s diet, I was inclined to agree.

Western methods for locating the bird have so far proven ineffective. A week of constant observation, camera trapping, and attempts to attract the bird by playing the call of its closest relative through a makeshift speaker we’ve dubbed the Bronzewing Blaster 5000 have amounted to nothing. Nor is history in our favor. In the late 1950s, zoologists Thomas and Margaret Gilliard spent three months within a few dozen kilometers of our camp, collecting some 500 specimens representing 98 species for the American Museum of Natural History. Among their findings were two species new to science. Absent was a single bronzewing. To our knowledge, no ornithologists have visited here since.

The Gilliard expedition was one of the final episodes of a heyday of scientific exploration in Melanesia that had a profound influence on the fields of ecology and evolution, arguably birthing theories such as island biogeography . This era ended in 1975, when Papua New Guinea gained independence and ended colonial license to travel freely in a region that now has near-complete Indigenous land tenure. In the interim, logging corporations felled the last grand forests of Borneo and Sumatra and began working their way through New Britain. Today, cost, logistics, lack of infrastructure, and sporadic violent crime discourage many foreign biologists from studying how the logging is affecting the island’s biodiversity.
